readings.title: Fifty Years
readings.challenge: Follow a long public poem as it shifts between celebration, argument, admission and hope.
readings.focus: A claim to full American citizenship, made on the fiftieth anniversary of emancipation.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. The title poem first appeared on 1 January 1913, fifty years after Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation took effect. Ken is range of sight; kraals are enclosed villages in southern Africa; Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native descent, was killed in the Boston Massacre of 1770; William Lloyd Garrison and Wendell Phillips were abolitionist speakers; John Brown led a raid against slavery in 1859; the editor Elijah Lovejoy was killed by a pro-slavery mob in 1837. “Daezd” is printed for “dazed.”
readings.contentNote: The poem recalls slavery and racial violence, and uses period language about Africa and about immigrants.

excerpt.locator: Fifty Years (1863–1913), the whole poem; opens “1863-1913”; closes “…of thousands fought, For which so many freely died, God cannot let it come to naught.”.

questions.prompt: Fifty years are “a winter’s day” in the history of a race, yet the speaker then looks back three centuries. How does changing the time scale change how the fifty years look?
facilitatorNotes: Against a people’s whole history, fifty years are brief; against the distance from the slave ship to citizenship, they mark an enormous journey. The double view both humbles and celebrates.
evidence: Just fifty years--a winter's day--
Look farther back! Three centuries!

questions.prompt: On what grounds does the speaker claim “This land is ours”? Find two different kinds of claim.
facilitatorNotes: By birth and by labour: Black workers cleared and farmed the land. And by service and loyalty: from Attucks onward, Black Americans have fought under the flag and never raised a hand against it.
evidence: This land is ours by right of birth, This land is ours by right of toil;
Was dyed by Attucks' willing blood.

questions.prompt: “And yet, my brothers, well I know.” What does the poem admit after its confident stanzas, and why include it?
facilitatorNotes: It names the violence, the waiting for justice and the moments when hope dies. The honesty makes the call to courage believable rather than empty cheer.
evidence: And yet, my brothers, well I know
To hear some voice for justice raised.

questions.prompt: How do the names in the last stanzas support the speaker’s hope?
facilitatorNotes: Garrison, Phillips, John Brown, Lovejoy and Lincoln gave their lives or voices to the cause; the speaker argues that such sacrifice cannot be undone. Readers may note that the ending offers faith rather than proof.
evidence: Think you their work can be undone?
God cannot let it come to naught.

questions.prompt: Some lines set Black Americans against “new-come foreign hordes” and describe Africa as “heathen kraals and jungle dens.” How do these phrases serve the poem’s argument, and how might a reader today respond?
facilitatorNotes: Johnson argues for full citizenship in the patriotic and religious language of 1913, including its prejudices about Africa and about immigrants. Readers can see the force of the argument and also its limits.
evidence: Stand back of new-come foreign hordes
From heathen kraals and jungle dens

readings.title: To America and O Black and Unknown Bards
readings.challenge: Read a poem made only of questions, then a sonnet-like ode that keeps asking “who” and “how.”
readings.focus: A question put to the nation, and praise for the nameless makers of the spirituals.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. “To America” is a short poem of questions to the nation. “O Black and Unknown Bards” honours the enslaved, unnamed people who created the spirituals, religious songs such as “Steal Away to Jesus,” “Roll, Jordan, Roll,” “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot,” “Nobody Knows the Trouble I See” and “Go Down, Moses.” A bard is a poet-singer; a lyre is a harp; “that great German master” is a celebrated European composer imagined dreaming the music of the Creation; a pean (paean) is a song of triumph; empyrean means heavenly.
readings.contentNote: The poems refer to slavery. To marvel at the singers’ achievement, Johnson uses period phrases such as “merely living clod” and “simple children of the sun and soil.”

excerpt.locator: To America and O Black and Unknown Bards, both whole poems; opens “How would you have us, as we are? Or sinking 'neath the load we bear? Our eyes fixed…”; closes “…live,--but more than this to you belongs: You sang a race from wood and stone to Christ.”.

questions.prompt: “To America” is made entirely of questions. What choice is it asking the nation to make, and why ask rather than tell?
facilitatorNotes: Whether Black Americans will rise as willing strength in the nation’s “wings” or be held down by tightening chains. The questions put the responsibility on America: “How would you have us?”
evidence: How would you have us, as we are?
Strong, willing sinews in your wings? Or tightening chains about your feet?

questions.prompt: In “O Black and Unknown Bards,” the speaker keeps asking “Who” and “How.” What amazes him?
facilitatorNotes: That people in bondage, denied schooling and freedom, made songs of such beauty and faith. The singer’s spirit “floated free” while chains stayed on his hands.
evidence: How came your lips to touch the sacred fire?
Though still about his hands he felt his chains.

questions.prompt: Why compare “Go Down, Moses” with the music of “that great German master”? What claim is the poem making?
facilitatorNotes: It sets the spirituals beside, even above, the greatest concert music: no theme is nobler, and their bars stir the blood like a trumpet call. The comparison claims the spirituals as high art.
evidence: Not that great German master in his dream
How like a mighty trumpet-call they stir

questions.prompt: “You sang far better than you knew.” What power does the last stanza give the songs? How do you read the final line?
facilitatorNotes: The songs outlived their singers and carried a people’s faith. The final line says the songs themselves turned a people from idols (“wood and stone”) to Christianity. Readers may discuss that religious framing as well as its praise of the singers’ lasting influence.
evidence: You sang far better than you knew;
You sang a race from wood and stone to Christ.

readings.title: O Southland! and To Horace Bumstead
readings.challenge: Hear love and criticism together in an address to the South, then a sonnet of encouragement to an ally.
readings.focus: A call to the South to leave the past behind, and a promise that no one fights for justice alone.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. Johnson grew up in Jacksonville, Florida. In his early adulthood, around 1900, Southern states were writing segregation and the denial of Black voting rights into law. Horace Bumstead was the white president of Atlanta University, where Johnson studied; the sonnet that follows is titled only with his name. A watchword is a motto; to shirk is to avoid; “withouten” is without.

excerpt.locator: O Southland! and the sonnet To Horace Bumstead, both whole poems; opens “O Southland! O Southland! Have you not heard the call, The trumpet blown, the word made…”; closes “…awful Sword of Justice in His hand,-- You shall not, no, you shall not, fight alone.”.

questions.prompt: What “gospel new” does “O Southland!” announce, and how is it different from a religious gospel?
facilitatorNotes: “Man shall be saved by man”: salvation through human cooperation and justice here and now, not only through faith in heaven.
evidence: Man shall be saved by man.
Salvation's present plan?

questions.prompt: What is the South clinging to in the third stanza, and why call it “a musty page”?
facilitatorNotes: An “idle age” of slavery and racial rank, as dead as an old book. Against it the poem sets springtime, work and a simple truth: “men are only men.”
evidence: To an idle age and a musty page, To a dead and useless thing?
And men are only men.

questions.prompt: The speaker calls it “my Southland” and “birthland.” How does that change the tone of his demand?
facilitatorNotes: He speaks as a son, not an outsider: the criticism comes with love. He redefines strength as helping the faint rather than pride.
evidence: O Southland! my Southland! O birthland! do not shirk
That he is strong who helps along The faint one at his side.

questions.prompt: The sonnet to Bumstead promises, “You shall not, no, you shall not, fight alone.” What discouragements does it name, and where does its comfort come from?
facilitatorNotes: Allies who lag behind and opponents whose “blind inertia” seems to undo every effort. The comfort comes from God’s justice, and the repeated “you shall not” makes the promise insistent.
evidence: Of blind inertia rendered as for naught
You shall not, no, you shall not, fight alone.

readings.title: The Color Sergeant
readings.challenge: Read a short ballad of a soldier’s death and find the argument hidden in its praise.
readings.focus: Honour for a Black soldier whom his country despised.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. On 1 July 1898, in the Spanish–American War, American troops stormed San Juan Hill in Cuba. Among them was the Tenth Cavalry, a Black regiment, the “sable Tenth” (sable means black). A color sergeant carries the regiment’s flag; a guidon is a small cavalry flag; to “present arms” is to salute with a weapon.
readings.contentNote: A soldier dies of his wounds in battle.

excerpt.locator: The Color Sergeant (On an Incident at the Battle of San Juan Hill), the whole poem; opens “(_On an Incident at the Battle of San Juan Hill_)”; closes “…a grim-like beauty; Despised of men for his humble race, Yet true, in death, to his duty.”.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza make the sergeant’s courage clear?
facilitatorNotes: He is first in the charge, carrying the flag, rushing where bullets (“leaden hail”) fall thickest without fear.
evidence: First in the charge up the fort-crowned hill
Not death nor danger fearing.

questions.prompt: “He closed his eyes on the bloody scene, / And presented arms to his Maker.” What is the effect of describing death as a military salute?
facilitatorNotes: Duty continues to the last moment: his death becomes a final act of discipline and faith, full of dignity.
evidence: And presented arms to his Maker.

questions.prompt: Look at “Black though his skin, yet his heart as true” and “Despised of men for his humble race.” Whose view of the soldier is the poem answering?
facilitatorNotes: The prejudiced view that Black soldiers were less loyal or brave. The “though … yet” shape argues against it. Readers today may notice that the line accepts the prejudice’s terms in order to refute them.
evidence: Black though his skin, yet his heart as true
Despised of men for his humble race

questions.prompt: He lies “without honor or rank.” Does the poem itself give him the honour he was denied? How?
facilitatorNotes: Yes: the title names his role, and the poem serves as his memorial, finding “a grim-like beauty” in his death. Some readers may ask whether a poem can make up for that neglect.
evidence: There he lay, without honor or rank
But, still, in a grim-like beauty

readings.title: Father, Father Abraham
readings.challenge: Read a short poem written for an anniversary and notice how it speaks for a whole people.
readings.focus: Gratitude to Lincoln, and a pledge to make emancipation worth its cost.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. Abraham Lincoln was born on 12 February 1809. Black Americans long marked his birthday in memory of the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863. To be “ransomed” is to be freed by a payment; to consecrate is to dedicate solemnly. The repeated address gives the poem the shape of a hymn or prayer.

excerpt.locator: Father, Father Abraham (On the Anniversary of Lincoln’s Birth), the whole poem; opens “(_On the Anniversary of Lincoln's Birth_)”; closes “…heart and brain, To send this judgment down the years: The ransom was not paid in vain.”.

questions.prompt: Why might the poem call Lincoln “Father” and speak of his “Christ-like love”? What kind of figure does he become?
facilitatorNotes: A patriarch and almost a saint, whose act freed his “children.” The religious language makes emancipation a kind of redemption. Readers may discuss whether such reverence simplifies history.
evidence: On us, the offspring of thy faith
The children of thy Christ-like love.

questions.prompt: The second stanza asks for Lincoln’s smile and for his patience. What does it admit?
facilitatorNotes: That the freed people and their children have achieved some things and fallen short in others. The pledge is honest about progress and failure.
evidence: For that which we have humbly wrought
Wherein we've failed or fallen short

questions.prompt: What “great price” was paid, and what does the speaker promise in return?
facilitatorNotes: The cost of the Civil War and of Lincoln’s own life. The promise is to live so that history judges “the ransom was not paid in vain,” an echo of Lincoln’s own words at Gettysburg.
evidence: Was paid, that we might ransomed be.
The ransom was not paid in vain.

questions.prompt: The poem speaks as “we” and “us” throughout. Who is the “we,” and why might a poet speak for a whole people on an anniversary?
facilitatorNotes: Black Americans, freed people and their children. An anniversary poem gives a community one voice for its memory and its commitment; “we consecrate ourselves” turns remembrance into a promise.
evidence: To-day we consecrate ourselves
Anew in hand and heart and brain

readings.title: Fragment
readings.challenge: Follow a single image through several stanzas and weigh a stern conclusion.
readings.focus: A prophecy that slavery’s wrong must be paid for.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. The poem is addressed to the white South. “Ten thousand thousand blacks” is about ten million, the Black population of the United States around 1910; the “twenty slaves in shackles bound” recall the first Africans brought to Virginia in 1619. To expiate is to atone; “fell” here means cruel; a sledge is a sledgehammer.
readings.contentNote: The poem warns that the punishment for slavery will fall even on “unborn children.”

excerpt.locator: Fragment, the whole poem; opens “The hand of Fate cannot be stayed, The course of Fate cannot be steered, By all the gods…”; closes “…that move in reverent awe; Forgiveness is an idle dream, God is not love, no, God is law.”.

questions.prompt: What does the wedge image say about the nation’s history?
facilitatorNotes: Slender at first, only twenty enslaved people, the wedge was forged by injustice and hatred, split the country in civil war, and still festers in the wound. The image ties slavery’s beginning to the whole national story.
evidence: A wedge so slender at the start--
And still lies cankering in the wound.

questions.prompt: The fourth stanza speaks to those who “bravely fought and died.” Whom does it mean, and what judgment does it pass?
facilitatorNotes: The soldiers of the Confederacy. Their courage, kept alive in Southern “story and song,” cannot redeem a wrong cause in the eyes of the future.
evidence: That though you bravely fought and died, You fought and died for what was wrong.

questions.prompt: The poem ends: “God is not love, no, God is law.” How does this differ from the usual Christian promise of forgiveness, and why might the poem insist on it?
facilitatorNotes: It rejects easy forgiveness: moral law works like the laws that move the planets, and wrongs must be paid for. The ending is a prophet’s warning. Readers may question the idea that guilt passes to “unborn children.”
evidence: Forgiveness is an idle dream, God is not love, no, God is law.
Nor shall their unborn children fail

questions.prompt: Why might Johnson title this poem “Fragment”?
facilitatorNotes: It may be a piece of a larger argument, a prophecy broken off, or part of a longer work. Its blunt start, with no introduction, supports the idea that it begins in the middle of something bigger.
evidence: The hand of Fate cannot be stayed

readings.title: The White Witch
readings.challenge: Read a poem as an allegory, deciding what its central figure might stand for without the poem naming it.
readings.focus: A beautiful, ageless danger, and a warning drawn from the speaker’s own experience.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. The speaker warns his “younger brothers” about a beautiful, ageless witch. Antaeus, in Greek myth, was a giant who grew stronger whenever he touched the earth; a blight is a disease that withers plants; “as the needle trembles to the pole” describes a compass needle pulled north. Readers often take the witch as an allegory for the dangerous allure, for Black men in the early 1900s, of the white world.
readings.contentNote: The poem uses sensual imagery. Many readers connect it with the deadly danger, in the era of lynching, of any relationship between a Black man and a white woman.

excerpt.locator: The White Witch, the whole poem; opens “O, brothers mine, take care! Take care! The great white witch rides out to-night, Trust…”; closes “…beauty bright; For in her glance there is a snare, And in her smile there is a blight.”.

questions.prompt: How does the witch differ from what the “younger brothers” expect? Why does that make her more dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: They expect a hag with snaggled teeth; she comes in the glowing charms of youth. Danger hidden inside beauty is harder to resist.
evidence: For ancient hag and snaggled tooth
In all the glowing charms of youth.

questions.prompt: What hides “back behind those smiling lips”? Explain the panther and the vampire.
facilitatorNotes: A predator and a creature that drains life. Under her caress lies hunger: she feeds on what she attracts.
evidence: The shadow of the panther lurks, The spirit of the vampire lies.

questions.prompt: “For I have seen the great white witch.” How does the speaker’s own experience give his warning authority?
facilitatorNotes: He has been drawn in and felt his strength ebb from his soul, and he “did not care.” The worst danger is that the victim consents.
evidence: For I have seen the great white witch
The strength go ebbing from my soul.

questions.prompt: What does the witch see in the young men that makes them her “prey”? What might she stand for?
facilitatorNotes: Their vitality, closeness to the earth and passion. She is ancient, “twin sister to the greedy earth,” and never named. Readers may see the white world’s allure, the danger surrounding interracial love in a violent time, or desire itself. Accept readings tied to the text.
evidence: She feels the old Antaean strength
And she has marked you for her prey.

questions.prompt: The poem begins and ends with nearly the same stanza. What has changed by the time we read it again?
facilitatorNotes: The warning now carries the weight of the speaker’s confession, and the new command, “beware! Look not upon her beauty bright,” is more urgent.
evidence: O, younger brothers mine, beware!
Look not upon her beauty bright

readings.title: The Young Warrior
readings.challenge: Hear a mother’s feelings through her son’s requests, though she never speaks.
readings.focus: Courage that asks not for safety but for steadfastness.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. A son speaks to his mother as he leaves to fight. “Gird me on my sword” means fasten it at my side; “Godspeed” is a wish for success; “unsullied” means unstained. The poem names neither war nor enemy; readers have taken it both as a soldier’s farewell and as a call to the struggle for justice.

excerpt.locator: The Young Warrior, the whole poem; opens “Mother, shed no mournful tears, But gird me on my sword; And give no utterance to thy…”; closes “…and purpose strong, My sword unsullied and ready to leap Unsheathed against the wrong.”.

questions.prompt: What does the son ask his mother not to do, and what does he ask instead?
facilitatorNotes: Not to weep or speak her fears, but to bless him and send prayers after him. He wants her strength, not her grief.
evidence: Mother, shed no mournful tears
But bless me with thy word.

questions.prompt: He asks her not to pray that he be kept from harm. What does he want her to pray for, and why?
facilitatorNotes: That he fight well and keep his purpose strong. Honour matters more to him than safety.
evidence: But pray not to defend from harm
Pray, rather, that with steadfast arm I fight the battle well.

questions.prompt: The poem never names the enemy, only “the wrong.” What is gained by leaving the cause unnamed?
facilitatorNotes: It can stand for any just struggle, including the fight against racial injustice, and it keeps the focus on moral purpose rather than on a particular war.
evidence: Unsheathed against the wrong.
A cause is to be won!

questions.prompt: How does the poem show the mother’s feelings without letting her speak?
facilitatorNotes: Through his requests: she is pale and frightened (“white and wan”), close to tears. Her silence is filled by what he asks her not to do.
evidence: Mother, look not so white and wan

readings.title: And the Greatest of These Is War
readings.challenge: Follow three speeches built on the same pattern and notice how the last breaks it.
readings.focus: Why war is worse than famine or plague: it turns people against each other.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. The title twists Saint Paul’s words, “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13). Famine, Pestilence and War are personified as scourges, punishments sent on humanity, reporting to Satan. A charnel-house holds dead bodies. The poem is written in long unrhymed lines (free verse); the book appeared in 1917, during the First World War.
readings.contentNote: The speakers describe death by famine, plague and war, including a hungry baby at its dead mother’s breast.

excerpt.locator: And the Greatest of These Is War, the whole poem; opens “Around the council-board of Hell, with Satan at their head, The Three Great Scourges of…”; closes “And Hell rang with the acclamation of the Fiends.”.

questions.prompt: What does each of the first two scourges boast about? How do Famine’s and Pestilence’s claims differ?
facilitatorNotes: Famine strikes the poor, the old and the helpless; Pestilence strikes great cities and the strongest, and wealth is no protection.
evidence: Great Prince, my brother, Famine, attacks the poor.
When I strike, neither their stores of gold or of grain avail.

questions.prompt: Why does War say his brothers have actually made people better?
facilitatorNotes: Their disasters awaken sympathy, brotherhood, love and the search for wisdom. War instead awakens “the demon and the brute” and turns brother against brother.
evidence: The God-like attributes of sympathy, of brotherhood and love
But I arouse in Man the demon and the brute

questions.prompt: How does the title twist Saint Paul’s line, and what does the change suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Paul’s greatest is charity, or love; Hell crowns War, love’s opposite. The irony makes war the anti-virtue.
evidence: O War, of all the scourges of humanity, I crown you chief.

questions.prompt: Satan nods twice and then smiles. How does the poem build to its climax?
facilitatorNotes: Two speeches end the same way; the third breaks the pattern with a smile, a crown and Hell’s cheering. Repetition makes the change land hard.
evidence: And Satan nodded his head.
And Satan smiled, stretched out his hand, and said

questions.prompt: War hauls people down “From the summit of fifty thousand years of upward climb.” What view of human history lies behind the image?
facilitatorNotes: History as a slow climb from beast to civilization, which war undoes in a moment, “back to the wolf.” Readers may ask whether history really climbs like that.
evidence: From the summit of fifty thousand years of upward climb
I set his teeth into his brother's throat.

readings.title: Sence You Went Away
readings.challenge: Hear how a single repeated phrase can carry a whole poem, and track where the poem’s attention moves.
readings.focus: Missing someone, in a song-like lament.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. This poem opens “Jingles & Croons,” the section in which Johnson wrote in the Black Southern dialect that poets such as Paul Laurence Dunbar had made popular. “Seems lak” means seems like; “sence” is since; “th’oat” is throat. Johnson later wrote that dialect verse had room for only two notes, humour and pathos.
readings.contentNote: The poem is written in a literary dialect of Black Southern speech, a convention of its period.

excerpt.locator: Sence You Went Away, the whole poem, the first of the Jingles & Croons; opens “Seems lak to me de stars don't shine so bright, Seems lak to me de sun done loss his…”; closes “…ma th'oat keeps gittin' dry, Seems lak to me a tear stays in ma eye, Sence you went away.”.

questions.prompt: Every line begins “Seems lak to me,” and every stanza ends “Sence you went away.” What does the repetition do to the feeling of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It circles like a lament or a song’s refrain: grief returns to the same thought and colours everything the speaker sees.
evidence: Seems lak to me dat ev'ything wants you
Sence you went away.

questions.prompt: The first stanzas describe the world; the last describes the speaker’s own body. Why move from the stars and sun to “ma th’oat” and “a tear”?
facilitatorNotes: The grief closes in from the sky to the throat and the eye. The most personal detail is saved for the end.
evidence: Seems lak to me de stars don't shine so bright
Seems lak to me a tear stays in ma eye

questions.prompt: The speaker says only that it “seems” the sun has lost its light. Why does the word matter?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker knows the change is in how things look to a grieving person, not in the world itself. That honesty makes the exaggeration touching rather than silly.
evidence: Seems lak to me de sun done loss his light

questions.prompt: Johnson later said dialect verse could express only humour and pathos. Does this poem support or challenge his view?
facilitatorNotes: It is pure pathos, simply done, which supports him; some readers feel the dialect gives intimacy and music, others that the convention limits the speaker. Both views can point to the poem’s plain repetitions.
evidence: Seems lak to me I don't know what to do

readings.title: Ghosts of the Old Year
readings.challenge: Listen to how the bell changes from a sound to a voice, and decide how hopeful the poem finally is.
readings.focus: New Year’s midnight as a reckoning with what was left undone.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. “Brazen” means made of brass, and also bold; “squandered” means wasted; “slighted gems and treasured clay” are valuable things neglected while worthless things were kept; a “blotted record” is a page spoiled with ink blots.

excerpt.locator: Ghosts of the Old Year, the whole poem; opens “The snow has ceased its fluttering flight, The wind sunk to a whisper light, An ominous…”; closes “…with aims unreached, life speeds Until the blotted record reads, "Failure!" at last.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza build up to the bell? What does the bell interrupt?
facilitatorNotes: The snow stops, the wind sinks, and “An ominous stillness” falls; the short line “A pause—a hush” holds the moment. Then the bell breaks the spell with loud, rolling sounds. The stillness makes the bell feel like a judgment.
evidence: An ominous stillness fills the night,
Loud, clanging mouthings of a bell,

questions.prompt: Why does the New Year bring the speaker “a sense of care / Akin to fright” rather than celebration?
facilitatorNotes: The bell announces a fresh page “On which to write,” but it also reminds him of what last year’s page holds. A new start makes him think of how earlier starts were wasted.
evidence: Brings to my heart a sense of care Akin to fright?
Another leaf before me spread On which to write.

questions.prompt: List the images of failure in the third stanza. What do they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Deeds not done, races never run, victories not won, barriers not leaped, fields not reaped: almost all are things that never happened. The regret is for chances not taken rather than for wrongs committed.
evidence: It tells the deeds that were not done,
Of fields unreaped.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with “Failure!” Is it a cry of despair, a warning, or something else?
facilitatorNotes: The pattern “Large resolutions, little deeds” leads to a final verdict on a whole life. Read as a warning, it urges the reader to act on this year’s fresh page; read as despair, it says the pattern never changes. Readers can test both against the opening of the fourth stanza.
evidence: Large resolutions, little deeds;
"Failure!" at last.

readings.title: “Lazy”
readings.challenge: Decide whether the speaker is joking, arguing seriously, or both.
readings.focus: A light-verse defense of leisure against a life of nothing but work.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. Light verse is playful, rhyming poetry on everyday subjects. “Pelf” is money, used scornfully; “drear” means dreary; ninety-three degrees Fahrenheit is about thirty-four Celsius; “spoil” here means riches; “sped” means over.

excerpt.locator: “Lazy,” the whole poem; opens “Some men enjoy the constant strife Of days with work and worry rife, But that is not my…”; closes “…short, as has been said, And we are such a long time dead, I'll spend my life in living.”.

questions.prompt: Why might the title be in quotation marks? Who calls the speaker lazy?
facilitatorNotes: The quotation marks suggest the word is other people’s label, which the speaker half accepts (“I fear that I am lazy”) and half mocks. The poem is his answer to the charge.
evidence: I fear that I am lazy.

questions.prompt: What kind of life does the speaker want? Which details make his picture comic?
facilitatorNotes: “A job of nothing much to do,” just enough money, no early mornings, and loafing by the sea in hot weather. The comedy is in the ordinary details anyone recognizes, like turning over at the six o’clock alarm, and in rhymes such as crazy/lazy.
evidence: A job of nothing much to do,
'Tis then I love to shift my ear,

questions.prompt: In the third stanza the speaker says work may have its use, “But still I feel that’s no excuse / For turning it into abuse.” What serious point is hidden in the joke?
facilitatorNotes: That work is good but can be overdone until people become like mules and life becomes all labor. The direct question to the reader (“What do you think about it?”) invites an argument.
evidence: But I'll not make myself a mule,
For turning it into abuse;

questions.prompt: “I’ll spend my life in living.” Is the last stanza a good argument, a lazy excuse, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He says gold is useless after death and life is short, so living matters more than earning. It is an old argument, and the speaker clearly enjoys making it; readers can grant the point about overwork while doubting that “nothing much to do” is the answer.
evidence: And we are such a long time dead,
I'll spend my life in living.

readings.title: The Word of an Engineer
readings.challenge: Separate the voices in the poem and decide how the speaker feels about trusting engineers.
readings.focus: Modern faith in machines and the people who design them.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. Keel is the bottom of a ship; the hulk is the hull; the Titans were giants of Greek myth; a draughtsman draws plans for buildings and machines. Johnson does not name a ship or a disaster.

excerpt.locator: The Word of an Engineer, the whole poem; opens “"She's built of steel From deck to keel, And bolted strong and tight; In scorn she'll…”; closes “…Without a thought of fear-- _Man never had The faith in God That he has in an engineer!_”.

questions.prompt: Who speaks the first two stanzas, which are in quotation marks? What claims are made about the ship?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like the builder or engineer, or the speaker repeating him: the ship is steel, “bolted strong and tight,” and can sail “In scorn” through any gale. The claims are confident to the point of boasting.
evidence: In scorn she'll sail The fiercest gale,
Ten thousand Titans' strength.

questions.prompt: What dangers do the ship and the train face? How do the images make them frightening?
facilitatorNotes: The “Ice Wolf” prowls the sea; the train flies “like a nightmare” into the tunnel’s “black-mouthed yawn” and over a bridge “Swung twixt the sky and hell.” The dangers are animals and monsters, while the passengers trust a thread of iron.
evidence: The Ice Wolf prowls,
Swung twixt the sky and hell,

questions.prompt: “Man never had / The faith in God / That he has in an engineer!” Is the ending admiring, critical, or both?
facilitatorNotes: It can praise human skill: one mind in “a draughtsman’s cell” makes the bridge that carries us all. It can also criticize misplaced faith, since people trust machines more than God. The italics and exclamation mark leave the tone for readers to judge.
evidence: Of the man in a draughtsman's cell.
That he has in an engineer!

questions.prompt: This book appeared in 1917, five years after the Titanic, a liner widely called unsinkable, struck an iceberg and sank. Does that fact change how you read the poem? Should it?
facilitatorNotes: Many readers will hear the “Ice Wolf” and the boast of “scorn” as ironic in the light of the Titanic. But the poem does not mention it, and it may have been written earlier. Ask readers to separate what the poem says from what history adds.
evidence: The Ice Wolf prowls,
But calm I sleep,

readings.title: Vashti
readings.challenge: Follow the speaker’s dream of a past life, then find the gulf he names in the present.
readings.focus: Longing across a distance of rank, time and something left unnamed.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. In the Bible’s Book of Esther, Vashti is a queen who refuses the king’s command to appear before his guests and is put aside; the poem never names her, so the title invites readers to connect the proud princess with her. The Southern Cross is a constellation of the southern sky; floss is fine silk thread; “crescent-wise” means curved like a new moon; “fervid” means burning; “lithe” means supple; “sinuous” means curving; a princess “of the blood” is royal by birth.

excerpt.locator: Vashti, the whole poem; opens “I sometimes take you in my dreams to a far-off land I used to know, Back in the ages long…”; closes “…than that which stood Between a princess of the blood and him who served low at her feet.”.

questions.prompt: Describe the “far-off land” of the dream. What kind of world is it?
facilitatorNotes: A land of palms, jeweled skies, a sapphire sea and a pyramid, where each day is “a poem chanted through.” It is an imagined, exotic past, too perfect to be real, which the speaker admits by calling it a dream.
evidence: a land of palms and languid streams.
each one a poem chanted through,

questions.prompt: What was the speaker in that life, and how did he feel about the princess? Find lines that show both worship and boldness.
facilitatorNotes: A serving lad who lived for her word of praise and dared only “stolen” glances, yet he notices her throat, her breast and her robe closely and imagines touching her sandals. His humility and his desire are mixed together.
evidence: And you were a princess in those days. And I--I was your serving lad.
I ventured many a stolen glance.

questions.prompt: Look at the crimson jewel that “turned to a living heart and bled.” Why does the speaker compare his own heart to it?
facilitatorNotes: The stone only imitates a wounded heart in the sunlight; his heart truly bled with hopeless love. The comparison turns her ornament into a symbol of his pain.
evidence: turned to a living heart and bled.
could never bleed as did my own!

questions.prompt: In the present, they are no longer princess and servant, yet he meets “a wider gulf.” What might the gulf be? How does the title help or complicate your answer?
facilitatorNotes: The poem does not say. It might be her indifference, a marriage or other tie, or the divisions of “this stern land.” If the princess is Vashti, the proud queen who refused a king, her pride may be part of the gulf. Readers should support their guess with the last stanza.
evidence: in this stern land we meet anew;
I meet a wider gulf than that which stood

readings.title: The Glory of the Day Was in Her Face
readings.challenge: Notice how the poem builds a portrait in two stanzas and then turns everything round in the third.
readings.focus: Grief that changes how the whole world looks.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. This short lyric uses ten-syllable lines rhymed in alternate pairs. Melodious means musical.

excerpt.locator: The Glory of the Day Was in Her Face, the whole poem; opens “The glory of the day was in her face, The beauty of the night was in her eyes. And over…”; closes “…To my dull ears, to my tear-blinded sight Are one with all the dead, since she is gone.”.

questions.prompt: What parts of the day and of nature does the speaker find in the woman in the first two stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: The glory of day in her face, the beauty of night in her eyes, morning’s blush, the dove’s call in her voice, the dawn light of love in her smile. She gathers the day’s beauty into one person.
evidence: The glory of the day was in her face,
And in her voice, the calling of the dove;

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the same day, night and birds return. What has happened to them, and why?
facilitatorNotes: To his “dull ears” and “tear-blinded sight” they are “one with all the dead, since she is gone.” Because she held their beauty, her death takes it out of the world. The last line shows the poem is an elegy, a poem of mourning.
evidence: To my dull ears, to my tear-blinded sight
Are one with all the dead, since she is gone.

questions.prompt: Why is the detail of the birds that “signal to their mates at dawn” especially painful?
facilitatorNotes: Birds calling to their mates remind him that he has lost his; nature goes on pairing while he is alone.
evidence: The birds that signal to their mates at dawn,

questions.prompt: Why might the poet wait until the last line to say “she is gone”? How does it change the first two stanzas when you reread them?
facilitatorNotes: The delay lets us share the delight before the loss; on rereading, the praise becomes memory. Some readers feel the surprise strongly; others notice that the very first word after “glory of the day” is “was.”
evidence: The glory of the day was in her face,
since she is gone

readings.title: A Mid-Day Dreamer
readings.challenge: Follow a daydream built from fairy-tale pictures, and decide what the dreamer is escaping from, or into.
readings.focus: The pleasure of letting the imagination steer.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. A craft is a boat; a galley is a ship moved by oars, in history often rowed by slaves or prisoners; the prow is the front of a boat; adown means down.

excerpt.locator: A Mid-Day Dreamer, the whole poem; opens “I love to sit alone, and dream, And dream, and dream; In fancy's boat to softly glide…”; closes “…idly back, And dream, and dream, And let them row me where they will Adown the stream.”.

questions.prompt: What is the dreamer’s boat made of? Why are all its materials so precious?
facilitatorNotes: Ivory, silver oars, sails spun of gold, gems on the prow, a hundred silken cords: a treasure that could exist only in fancy. The riches show that the dream is pure wish.
evidence: My craft is built of ivory,
The sails are spun of golden threads,

questions.prompt: Who rows the boat, and what keeps them in time? What mood do these details create?
facilitatorNotes: Sprightly elves, keeping time to music sung by mermaids combing their hair: a fairy-tale world where work is light and musical. Readers may notice that “galley-slaves” is a harsh word for such cheerful rowers, and ask what it does in a dream of ease.
evidence: My galley-slaves are sprightly elves
Made by the mermaids as they comb

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza echo the first? What does “let them row me where they will” suggest about this kind of dreaming?
facilitatorNotes: “And dream, and dream” returns, and the dreamer lies back and gives up control. The poem praises idle, drifting imagination; readers may find it restful, or notice that the title sets it at mid-day, when most people are working.
evidence: And I the while lie idly back,
And let them row me where they will

readings.title: The Ghost of Deacon Brown
readings.challenge: Enjoy a comic ballad’s bouncing rhythm, and find the lesson under the joke.
readings.focus: A miser’s gold, a ghost and a town that empties.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. A deacon is an officer of a church; a miser hoards money; phosphorescent means glowing; “for let” means for rent.

excerpt.locator: The Ghost of Deacon Brown, the whole poem; opens “In a backwoods town Lived Deacon Brown, And he was a miser old; He would trust no bank,…”; closes “And the town is now for let, But the ghost is digging yet.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Deacon Brown bury his gold, and what goes wrong?
facilitatorNotes: He trusts no bank, buries the box, and the very next day forgets where; he searches until he falls sick and dies. The miser’s distrust defeats itself.
evidence: He would trust no bank,
He forgot just where he hid it:

questions.prompt: What does the ghost do, and why does it laugh?
facilitatorNotes: It digs every foot of ground with a spade, still searching, and laughs “in ghostly glee” when people run away. The ghost is as greedy, and as alone, as the living man.
evidence: With a spade it dug each foot of ground;
it would laugh in ghostly glee.

questions.prompt: How do the short lines and repeated words make the poem funny? Point to a place where the rhythm does the joking.
facilitatorNotes: Short rhyming lines (“In a backwoods town / Lived Deacon Brown”) bounce like a nursery rhyme, and repeats such as “Down deep in the ground a box of gold” and “Hee, hee!” add to the fun. The light rhythm keeps a death and a haunting from feeling grim.
evidence: In a backwoods town
Down deep in the ground a box of gold.

questions.prompt: The poem ends “the town is now for let, / But the ghost is digging yet.” What is the lesson, and who pays for the deacon’s greed?
facilitatorNotes: Greed outlasts death and ruins a whole town: people leave and the place goes “quickly down.” Some readers draw a moral about hoarding; others simply enjoy the picture of digging that never ends.
evidence: Went quickly down,
But the ghost is digging yet.

readings.title: Five Love Lyrics
readings.challenge: Compare five short love poems, and notice how each finds a different image for the same feeling.
readings.focus: Love seen through the times of day, a pair of eyes, a rose and a bee, a safe harbour and a goddess’s garland.
readings.context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a Black American poet, lawyer, diplomat and civil-rights leader who wrote the words of “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” published Fifty Years and Other Poems in 1917. These five lyrics stand together in the book. To swoon is to faint; a blight is a withering; “glamouring” means enchanting; a “quested goal” is the goal of a search; a haven is a safe harbour; Venus is the Roman goddess of love; “embowered” means sheltered by leafy branches; a garden close is an enclosed garden.

excerpt.locator: Morning, Noon and Night; Her Eyes Twin Pools; The Awakening; Beauty That Is Never Old; Venus in a Garden; the five poems whole; opens “When morning shows her first faint flush, I think of the tender blush That crept so…”; closes “…that for love had bled; And the goddess made a garland Gathered from the roses red.”.

questions.prompt: In “Morning, Noon and Night,” what memory does each time of day bring back? Why does the poem end in darkness?
facilitatorNotes: Morning’s flush recalls her first blush, noon’s roses her hair and embrace, night her tear-dimmed eyes asking him to stay “Although your lips sent me away.” The love story runs from dawn to its end, so the last night is dark.
evidence: Their mute entreaty that I stay,
And dark--so dark becomes the night.

questions.prompt: What warning is hidden in “Her Eyes Twin Pools”?
facilitatorNotes: The eyes are beautiful pools of “mystic light,” but a man who bends to gaze may “plunge, and lose his soul.” Love’s pull is also a danger; readers may think of the old story of Narcissus or simply of losing oneself.
evidence: A man might plunge, and lose his soul.

questions.prompt: In “The Awakening” the speaker dreams of being a rose and the beloved a bee. What does the speaker understand only at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The rose waited and grew without knowing why; when the bee comes, “then I knew / That I had waited there for you.” Love gives meaning, after the fact, to a lonely life.
evidence: Just why I waited there and grew.
That I had waited there for you.

questions.prompt: Compare “Beauty That Is Never Old” with “Venus in a Garden.” Which beauty lasts, and why does Venus choose the red roses?
facilitatorNotes: In the first, the beauty in the beloved’s loving eyes is a haven that never ages; Venus chooses red roses because they took their colour “From the hearts that for love had bled.” One poem finds love a comfort, the other a cost; readers may prefer either.
evidence: The only beauty that is never old.
From the hearts that for love had bled;
